Use you and your when translating abstract systems into immediate consequences, especially in examples, warnings, and closing demands."},"first-person-plural-family":{"prose":"First-person plural shifts between inclusive solidarity and collective exposure: we can name ordinary people facing a system, or a shared public obligation to resist it. Use we and us to widen a concrete example into a common stake, without making the readership anonymous."},"contractions":{"prose":"Contractions keep the argumentative voice conversational and brisk, even when the subject is technical or politically serious. Use them in explanation, transitions, and direct address; reserve more formal phrasing for quoted language, defined terms, or deliberate emphasis."},"uncontracted-negatives":{"prose":"Full negative forms appear as occasional points of emphasis rather than the default negative register. Use do not, cannot, or similar forms when slowing a sentence to mark a firm distinction, expose a false premise, or sharpen a concluding judgment."},"profanity-vulgarity":{"prose":"Profanity and vulgarity function as targeted intensifiers, ridicule, and anti-euphemistic punctuation around institutional abuse or absurdity. Place them selectively at a turn, punchline, or verdict after the reasoning has made the target clear; do not let them replace the explanation."},"first-person-singular-family":{"prose":"Singular self-reference presents the writer as an arguer, reader of sources, and occasional participant whose experience supplies a concrete scale for broader claims. Use I or my to frame an observation, disclose a relevant example, or mark a considered judgment, not to turn the piece into autobiography."},"question-marks":{"prose":"Questions are used rhetorically to expose contradictions, test a sales pitch, or make the reader perform an obvious inference; they are usually answered immediately by the surrounding argument. Place them at pivots and challenge points, with occasional genuine prompts embedded in explanation."},"round-parenthetical-spans":{"prose":"Parentheses carry compact asides, qualifications, comic labels, and supplementary facts without interrupting the main argumentative line. Use them for material that enriches or colors a sentence but can be bracketed off; keep the governing claim readable if the aside is removed."},"em-dashes":{"prose":"The corpus does not establish em-dashes as a supported interruption device. For pivots, asides, or abrupt qualifications, use the observed alternatives—especially parentheses or the established dash form—rather than introducing this mark as a default."},"en-dashes":{"prose":"En-dashes support interruption, contrast, and compressed qualification inside otherwise forceful sentences.
